parts.title: Reserving a campsite
parts.context: A man phones a campsite to book a pitch for a group of friends.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning a campsite to reserve a pitch for a group. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: beth
script.text: Riverbend Campsite, Beth speaking.

script.speaker: oscar
script.text: Hello. I'd like to reserve a place for a group of friends. We'll be coming in tents.

script.speaker: beth
script.text: Lovely. I'll take some details, and then I'll tell you what's available.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The caller will be coming in tents, so 'tents' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: beth
script.text: Could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: oscar
script.text: It's Oscar Lindqvist. That's L-I-N-D-Q-V-I-S-T.

script.speaker: beth
script.text: Thank you, Mr Lindqvist. And when would you like to arrive?

script.speaker: oscar
script.text: On the nineteenth of July, if that's possible.

script.speaker: beth
script.text: Yes, we have space on that date. How long are you staying?

script.speaker: oscar
script.text: Four nights. We'd leave on the Sunday morning.

script.speaker: beth
script.text: And how many of you are there?

script.speaker: oscar
script.text: I thought eight, but two friends have dropped out, so there will be six of us.

script.speaker: beth
script.text: Fine. Are you coming by car?

script.speaker: oscar
script.text: Two cars, actually, and one of them will be pulling a small trailer, for the tents and the cooking equipment.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: beth
script.text: A trailer is no problem, but I'd put you on the field near the river, because the ground is flat there, and it's easy to park. The field by the woods is sloping.

script.speaker: oscar
script.text: The river sounds great. How much is it?

script.speaker: beth
script.text: Twenty-four pounds a night for the whole group. That's the high-season rate. In June it was twenty-two, but in July and August it goes up.

script.speaker: oscar
script.text: That's reasonable. Is electricity available?

script.speaker: beth
script.text: Yes, we can offer an electric hook-up for an extra five pounds a night, though most people with tents don't need it.

script.speaker: oscar
script.text: No, we'll manage. Are there any rules we should know about?

script.speaker: beth
script.text: Quiet hours start at ten in the evening, so please keep the noise down after that. And rubbish should be put in the bins next to the campsite shop. Don't leave bags outside your tent, because the foxes will find them.

script.speaker: oscar
script.text: Understood. Thank you very much.

script.speaker: beth
script.text: I'll send you a confirmation by email. We look forward to seeing you.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A new tram line
parts.context: A council officer explains plans for a tram line at a public meeting.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a council officer presenting plans for a new tram line at a public meeting. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: hayes
script.text: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming. I'm Sarah Hayes, from the city council's transport department, and I'm here to tell you about the new tram line.

script.speaker: hayes
script.text: Some people believe that the first trams will run next spring, but that is far too optimistic. The line will open in two years' time, at the end of the construction period.

script.speaker: hayes
script.text: The new line is twelve kilometres long, and it will connect the university in the north with the airport in the south, passing through the city centre. There will be eighteen stops, and each tram can carry about two hundred and fifty passengers.

script.speaker: hayes
script.text: The journey from the university to the airport will take thirty-five minutes. By bus, it's currently about fifty minutes, and in rush hour it can be even longer.

script.speaker: hayes
script.text: The project will cost about three hundred million pounds. Most of that, roughly two thirds, will come from a grant from the national government, and the rest will be paid by the city council, with a small contribution from local businesses.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: hayes
script.text: What benefits can we expect? The council expects the trams to take up to ten thousand car journeys off the roads every day, so there should be less traffic in the city centre. We also expect air quality to improve, as the trams are electric and produce no exhaust fumes.

script.speaker: hayes
script.text: Tickets will cost the same as the buses, so I'm afraid there will be no reduction in fares. And we're not planning extra car parks, because we want people to leave their cars at home.

script.speaker: hayes
script.text: Several residents have asked about the trees along Park Avenue. Thirty trees will have to be removed to make space for the tracks, but we will plant sixty new ones, in the same street and in the nearby park.

script.speaker: hayes
script.text: Building work begins in September, starting with the northern section near the university. Road closures will be announced at least a month before.

script.speaker: hayes
script.text: We would like to know what you think, and there is an online survey on the council's website, which will be open until the end of next month. You are also welcome to ask questions now. Who would like to start?

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Designing an energy-efficient house
parts.context: Two architecture students plan a low-energy house.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two architecture students, Lena and Omar, planning a design for an energy-efficient house. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: lena
script.text: Omar, have you read the brief for the housing project again? It says the house has to be for a family of four, on a small plot.

script.speaker: omar
script.text: Yes, and there's a budget of two hundred thousand pounds. That's the part that worries me.

script.speaker: lena
script.text: I think we should use timber for the frame. It stores carbon, and it's quick to build.

script.speaker: omar
script.text: I agree, but I'm not sure about the outside walls. Local stone looks lovely, but it's expensive.

script.speaker: lena
script.text: Then let's use timber cladding as well, from sustainable forests. It's cheaper, and it's lighter.

script.speaker: omar
script.text: Fine. Now the roof. Should we have a green roof or solar panels?

script.speaker: lena
script.text: Both would be too heavy. A green roof helps wildlife, but panels would produce electricity, which the brief rewards. I'd choose the panels.

script.speaker: omar
script.text: OK. Now, orientation. The main windows should face south.

script.speaker: lena
script.text: Yes, but there's a tall building to the south of our plot, and it blocks the winter sun.

script.speaker: omar
script.text: Then we could tilt the roof and put the living room on the first floor, where it gets more light.

script.speaker: lena
script.text: Clever. We'd put the bedrooms downstairs, then. I think Dr Kaplan will like that.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: omar
script.text: Now, the heating. How do we keep the house warm without a boiler?

script.speaker: lena
script.text: It's based on the passive house idea. First, large south-facing windows, triple glazed, so that they let the winter sun in without losing heat.

script.speaker: omar
script.text: Then the walls. We need very thick insulation, about forty centimetres, so the heat stays inside.

script.speaker: lena
script.text: The problem is that a sealed house needs fresh air, so we have a ventilation system, which brings air in and takes stale air out.

script.speaker: omar
script.text: And the clever part is the heat exchanger. The outgoing air warms the incoming air as they pass, so almost no heat is lost.

script.speaker: lena
script.text: On the very coldest days, there's a small pump, which takes heat from the ground, and that provides the rest.

script.speaker: omar
script.text: We won't need a battery, then?

script.speaker: lena
script.text: Not for the heating. Perhaps for the solar panels, but that's a separate question. Shall we draw it?

script.speaker: omar
script.text: Let's start with the floor plan.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: endangered languages
parts.context: A linguistics lecture on why languages disappear and how some are revived.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about endangered languages. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good afternoon. There are about seven thousand languages spoken in the world today. But linguists estimate that around half of them could disappear by the end of this century. A language is usually called endangered when children stop learning it, and the last speakers are mostly elderly.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Why does this happen? Sometimes it is the result of deliberate policy. In many countries, children were forced to use the national language at school, and were punished for speaking their home language. Another cause is migration to cities, where jobs often require a dominant language, so that parents decide not to pass their own language to their children. And then there is the influence of media, which are dominated by a small number of big languages.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Why does it matter? Every language carries knowledge. Communities that have lived in one place for centuries often have words for local plants and animals, and for their uses in medicine, that science has never recorded. When the language disappears, the knowledge disappears too, together with a way of describing the world, and a sense of identity.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Can a language be saved? There are some encouraging examples. Hebrew was used mainly for religious purposes for nearly two thousand years, but it was revived in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, and today it has millions of native speakers.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: In New Zealand, the Maori community started language nests in nineteen eighty-two. These are nurseries where very young children are taught entirely in Maori by elders. Many of the children who attended became fluent, and later sent their own children to Maori-medium schools.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: In Wales, the long decline in the number of Welsh speakers has slowed, thanks to teaching in schools and to a Welsh-language television channel. And modern technology helps too, with apps, online dictionaries and recordings of the last speakers.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: But experts agree that dictionaries alone are not enough. A language survives only if it is used in daily life, at home, with friends and at work. That is the real challenge. Next week we'll look at how new words are created.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
